items.readable_text:
Content:
When we multiply the argument of [MATH: y=\sin x] by some number [MATH: B,] the resulting function [MATH: y=\sin(Bx)] is a horizontal scaling of the original graph by a scaling factor [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B}.] More specifically, it is said to be

Content:
- a horizontal stretch if [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B} > 1,] or
- a horizontal shrink if [MATH: 0 < \dfrac{1}{B} < 1.]

Content:
In general, the period of [MATH: y=\sin (Bx)] is equal to the period of [MATH: y=\sin x] (which is [MATH: 2\pi]) multiplied by the scaling factor:
[MATH: \text{period} = 2\pi\cdot \dfrac{1}{B}]

Content:
For example, consider the graph of [MATH: \displaystyle y=\sin{2x}] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=2,] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal shrink with period [MATH: 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \pi.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0b63cbb505b8d86fbd09fe68d597a3bb]

Content:
On the other hand, consider the graph of [MATH: y=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=\dfrac{1}{2},] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)} = 2.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal stretch with period [MATH: 2\pi \cdot 2 = 4\pi.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bd4675256fcec00706a447f8a1e93b14]

sections.normalized_html:

So, the period is

[MATH: 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B} = 2\pi \cdot 2= 4\pi.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order to find the value of [MATH: B,] we first need to find the period of the function.

From the graph, we can see that function makes [MATH: 3] complete cycles on the interval [MATH: [0,2\pi].] So, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.]

We know that for a function [MATH: y=\sin (Bx),] the horizontal scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B},] and the period is multiplied by the scaling factor: [MATH: \text{period} = 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B}]

For our particular function, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3},] so we have

[MATH: (2π)/(3)|= 2π ⋅ (1)/(B); (2π)/(3)|= (2π)/(B); B|= 3.]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{x}{4} \right),] what is the graph of the curve [MATH: y=f(x)?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{x}{4} \right),] what is the graph of the curve [MATH: y=f(x)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order to graph the function, it's helpful to know the period. In order to determine the period, we first need to determine the scaling factor.

Notice that the function [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{x}{4} \right)] can be written as [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{1}{4} x \right).] So, it takes the form [MATH: y=\tan (Bx)] with [MATH: B = \dfrac{1}{4}.]

The horizontal scaling factor is given by [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B} = \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)} = 4.]

So, the period is

[MATH: \pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B} = \pi \cdot 4 = 4\pi.]

Now that we know the period is [MATH: 4\pi,] we can draw the general shape of the tangent function, but stretch it so that it fills up the interval [MATH: (-2\pi, 2\pi).]

The resulting graph is shown below.

When we multiply the argument of [MATH: y=\sin x] by some number [MATH: B,] the resulting function [MATH: y=\sin(Bx)] is a horizontal scaling of the original graph by a scaling factor [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B}.] More specifically, it is said to be

Content:
- a horizontal stretch if [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B} > 1,] or
- a horizontal shrink if [MATH: 0 < \dfrac{1}{B} < 1.]

Content:
In general, the period of [MATH: y=\sin (Bx)] is equal to the period of [MATH: y=\sin x] (which is [MATH: 2\pi]) multiplied by the scaling factor:
[MATH: \text{period} = 2\pi\cdot \dfrac{1}{B}]

Content:
For example, consider the graph of [MATH: \displaystyle y=\sin{2x}] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=2,] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal shrink with period [MATH: 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \pi.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0b63cbb505b8d86fbd09fe68d597a3bb]

Content:
On the other hand, consider the graph of [MATH: y=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=\dfrac{1}{2},] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)} = 2.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal stretch with period [MATH: 2\pi \cdot 2 = 4\pi.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bd4675256fcec00706a447f8a1e93b14]

Item 2 — Example: Determining the Period of a Stretched Sine or Cosine Function

Example Prompt:
What is the period of [MATH: y=\cos\left(\dfrac x 2\right)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, note that the function [MATH: y=\cos\left(\dfrac x 2\right)] can be written as [MATH: y=\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{2} x\right).] So, it takes the form [MATH: y=\cos(Bx)] with [MATH: B = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

The horizontal scaling factor is given by

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{B} = \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) } = 2.]

So, the period is

[MATH: 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B} = 2\pi \cdot 2= 4\pi.]

We can verify this in the graph shown below:

Item 5 — Example: Identifying the Missing Parameter Given the Graph of a Stretched Sine or Cosine Function

Example Prompt:
The graph below is generated by the function [MATH: y=\sin(Bx).] Find the value of [MATH: B.]

[IMG: /graphics/56e09f93b3f748dd31f5715d44f4f834]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In order to find the value of [MATH: B,] we first need to find the period of the function.

From the graph, we can see that function makes [MATH: 3] complete cycles on the interval [MATH: [0,2\pi].] So, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.]

[IMG: /graphics/21a1c6550960494da28a4bbff3b448c4]

We know that for a function [MATH: y=\sin (Bx),] the horizontal scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B},] and the period is multiplied by the scaling factor:
[MATH: \text{period} = 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B}]

For our particular function, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3},] so we have

[MATH: (2π)/(3)|= 2π ⋅ (1)/(B); (2π)/(3)|= (2π)/(B); B|= 3.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Horizontal Stretches of the Tangent Function

Content:
Graphs of tangent can be horizontally scaled in the same way as graphs of sine and cosine. The only difference is that the period of [MATH: y=\tan x] is [MATH: \pi] (rather than [MATH: 2\pi]), so the period of [MATH: y= \tan(Bx)] is

Content:
[MATH: \text{period} = \pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B}.]

Content:
For example, consider the graph of [MATH: y=\tan(2x)] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=2,] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal shrink with period [MATH: \pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/798106f5bbff7f75138a89c7c8421945]

Content:
On the other hand, consider the graph of [MATH: y=\tan\left( \dfrac{1}{2}x \right)] shown below. For this function, we have [MATH: B=\dfrac{1}{2},] so the scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)} = 2.] Consequently, the function is a horizontal stretch with period [MATH: \pi \cdot 2 = 2\pi.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/79c5b9ab74a11ab51a2d64ffab44f941]

Item 9 — Example: Identifying the Graph of a Stretched Tangent Function

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{x}{4} \right),] what is the graph of the curve [MATH: y=f(x)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In order to graph the function, it's helpful to know the period. In order to determine the period, we first need to determine the scaling factor.

Notice that the function [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{x}{4} \right)] can be written as [MATH: f(x) = \tan \left( \dfrac{1}{4} x \right).] So, it takes the form [MATH: y=\tan (Bx)] with [MATH: B = \dfrac{1}{4}.]

The horizontal scaling factor is given by
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{B} = \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)} = 4.]

So, the period is

[MATH: \pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B} = \pi \cdot 4 = 4\pi.]

Now that we know the period is [MATH: 4\pi,] we can draw the general shape of the tangent function, but stretch it so that it fills up the interval [MATH: (-2\pi, 2\pi).]

The resulting graph is shown below.

Item 12 — Example: Identifying the Missing Parameter Given the Graph of a Stretched Tangent Function

Example Prompt:
The graph below shows [MATH: y=\tan(Bx).] What is the value of [MATH: B?]

[IMG: /graphics/281ae2174e6345fbae065a1c5cc9d3a5]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In order to find the value of [MATH: B,] we first need to find the period of the function.

From the graph, we can see that function makes [MATH: 3] complete cycles on the interval [MATH: (-\pi,\pi).] So, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.]

[IMG: /graphics/adcf1196cace39091e5dc9b25d320c4e]

We know that for a function [MATH: y=\tan (Bx),] the horizontal scaling factor is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{B},] and the period is multiplied by the scaling factor:
[MATH: \text{period} = \pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{B}]

For our particular function, the period is [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3},] so we have

[MATH: (2π)/(3)|= π ⋅ (1)/(B); (2)/(3)|= (1)/(B); B|= (3)/(2).]
